object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A business entity that signs up for subscriptions. Each account is identified by a unique six-digit account number that is never reused, even if the same company returns.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off. Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.
Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A unique six-digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused even if the account is later closed and reopened.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off. Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement between an account and the company for payment of a specified amount on a specified cycle for a specified product. Each subscription has a subscription ID, belongs to exactly one account and one product, and has a current price plan, start date, optional end date, billing period, and status.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID. Which is unique? Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.
Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan. Start date. End date, sometimes. Billing period. Status.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: A unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with 'SUB'.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID. Which is unique? Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product that can be subscribed to. Currently there are three products: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: And products -- how are they identified? Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artifact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. Examples include CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490. Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing. And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: A code that uniquely identifies a price plan.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing what the customer gets: a feature set including the number of seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. Examples are Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.

object_types.name: BundleName

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription becomes effective. Every subscription has a start date.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription expires or is cancelled. Optional for open-ended subscriptions, mandatory for fixed-term subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: End date sometimes? An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing frequency for a subscription. Must be exactly one of: Monthly or Annual.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual. Only those two. Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it. Can a subscription be both? No. It's one or the other. You cannot bill someone monthly and annually for the same subscription, that's just billing them twice. And it's never neither? Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current status of a subscription. Exactly one of: Trialing, Active, PastDue, Cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Status? Trialing, active, past due, cancelled. Four. Every subscription in exactly one? Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan. Belongs to exactly one subscription and records the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested the change.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history. So a plan change is its own thing, with its own identity? It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month. And a plan change belongs to exactly one subscription? One change, one subscription. It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: Plan Change Initiation vs. Effective Date Discrepancy: The transcript indicates that a plan change can be requested on one date and take effect on a different date (e.g., 'Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month'). However, it is unclear whether there is a separate 'RequestDate' attribute on PlanChange, or whether the system only tracks the EffectiveDate and the Requester. The model captures EffectiveDate and Requester but does not include a RequestDate. Should PlanChange have both a request date and an effective date?

source_references.excerpt: It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

ambiguities.description: Current Plan Derivation and Maintenance: The transcript states that the subscription's current plan is 'derived from the change history' but also notes that there is a denormalized 'current_plan' field on the subscription record that is 'maintained by the change process'. It is unclear whether the current plan field should be modeled as a stored attribute or as a derived computation. The model currently treats it as stored, but clarification is needed: Is current_plan the system of record, or should it always be recomputed from plan changes if they disagree?

source_references.excerpt: We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history. No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Subscription Status and Paused Flag Overlap: The transcript notes that 'Paused' is a separate boolean flag that 'behaves like a status' and that querying for 'active subscriptions' incorrectly includes paused ones. The model captures only the four explicit statuses (Trialing, Active, PastDue, Cancelled) and does not include a Paused attribute. Should the model capture the Paused flag as a separate boolean attribute on Subscription? If so, what are the valid combinations of Status and Paused?

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. It behaves like a status. It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too. I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly. I'm not going to invent a fifth status you don't have.

ambiguities.description: Mid-Term Cancellation Refund Policy: The transcript discusses a disagreement between Tom (Product), Priya (Billing), and Sam (Revenue) about whether mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions should result in a refund, prorated refund, or credit. The facilitator parks this decision explicitly, noting it must be resolved by finance and legal. The current system behavior is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to the paid-through date with no automatic refund mechanism. However, manual credits were issued four times in the previous quarter. The model captures the system behavior but not the unresolved business rule. Should the model include a RefundPolicy or RefundAmount attribute, or is the current lack of formalized refund mechanism the accurate capture?

source_references.excerpt: That's not what the pricing page implies and it's not what sales tell people. It becomes one when the customer escalates and we give them a refund anyway, which we did four times last quarter. Then let's write a policy. But I'm not inventing one in this room. So the system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule. The model will capture the system behaviour, which is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: Plan Terminology Ambiguity: The transcript identifies three different uses of the word 'plan': (1) Price Plan (e.g., CORE-MO-49), identified by plan code and specifying price and billing frequency; (2) Feature Bundle (e.g., Professional), identified by name and specifying features/seats/API/SSO; (3) Sales Deal Plan (mentioned briefly, referring to custom negotiated deals). The model distinguishes PricePlan and FeatureBundle, but does not capture the Sales Deal Plan concept. Is the Sales Deal Plan a third entity type that should be modeled, or is it out of scope for this system model?

source_references.excerpt: Now, plan. You both used the word. Priya, what's a plan? The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing. That's not what I mean by plan at all. When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. We've got two things both called plan. We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither. Don't. That's a different meeting.

ambiguities.description: End Date Optionality and Cancellation: The model captures that EndDate is optional (most subscriptions are open-ended and run until cancelled, while enterprise deals may have a fixed end date). However, the transcript also discusses that when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term, the system 'sets the end date to the paid-through date'. This implies that cancellation causes an EndDate to be populated. Is the EndDate truly optional in the data model, or does cancellation make it mandatory? Should there be a separate 'CancellationDate' or 'PaidThroughDate' attribute?

source_references.excerpt: End date sometimes? An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal. There's a system behaviour: cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues.

ambiguities.description: MRR Derivation and Reporting: The transcript states that MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is 'derived' and 'worked out' from the price plan and billing period (e.g., an annual plan at 490 yields MRR of 40.83). The facilitator explicitly decides not to model MRR as a stored attribute because it is derived. However, Sam mentions that MRR appears in 'the reporting layer' and that he 'lives in' this number for revenue analysis. Is there a separate MRR table or view in the reporting schema, or is MRR computed on-the-fly from Subscription and PricePlan? The model does not include MRR as an attribute or fact type -- is this correct?

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in. It's on the subscription in the reporting layer. That's not quite what I asked. In the source system, is MRR a field somebody sets, or is it worked out? ...It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83. I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: Product Existence and Future States: The transcript mentions that there are currently three products (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) with a fourth in discovery. The model captures ProductCode with a value constraint listing the three current products. Should the value constraint be updated when the fourth product is released, or should ProductCode be open-ended? Is the enumerated value constraint appropriate, or should products be managed as a dynamic entity?

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three? Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Feature Bundle Lifecycle and Pricing: The transcript notes that feature bundles can exist without any price plan pointing to them (e.g., Enterprise existed for two months before pricing was finalized). This creates a state where a FeatureBundle has no corresponding PricePlan. Should the model include a constraint that at least one PricePlan must eventually entitle a FeatureBundle, or is the current optional relationship (many PricePlans to one FeatureBundle, zero or more) the correct capture?

source_references.excerpt: Can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it? Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Account Closure and Reactivation: The transcript states that account numbers are 'never reused' and that if 'the same company comes back' after closing an account, 'they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.' This raises the question: should there be an explicit Account status (e.g., Active, Closed) or relationship tracking (e.g., 'CompanyLegalEntity has multiple Accounts over time')? The model does not capture the notion of a closed account or link historical accounts of the same company.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: Halloway Group Incident Constraints: The transcript recounts an incident where Halloway Group had two subscriptions to the same product (analytics) on the same account billed for eight months before detection. The constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' was implemented at the database level to prevent recurrence. However, the model does not capture whether this constraint was violated in the historical data or how such data is handled. Is the constraint retroactive or only forward-looking?

source_references.excerpt: A customer -- Halloway Group -- had someone in their finance team and someone in their engineering team both sign up for the analytics product, on the same account, three weeks apart. Different plans. We billed them twice for eight months and neither of them noticed because the invoices went to different cost centres. When they did notice, we refunded the lot and it was about sixty thousand. One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level. Yes.
